attribution.note: Marcus states it in his own voice and credits Karla Ortiz with the same point. 'As X noted' adopts the view, so it is his claim.

semantics.note: The context is AI regulation. 'Default' can mean a tendency that holds unless something resists it, not only a measured prevalence. The normalisation keeps this broad general wording.

contract.note: Reading 'default' as the usual pattern is ordinary. A one-day snapshot is an evaluator choice. Under either reading of 'default', the packet lacks representative evidence, so the interpretation does not change the result.

evidence.note: The DHS announcement shows AI executives sitting on an advisory board. It shows access, not captured decisions or a pattern across AI regulation.
A 2024 peer-reviewed interview study identifies channels of industry influence. Its sample is small and non-random, so it does not establish how common capture is.
This 2026 preprint, available before the cutoff, counts capture mechanisms in news articles from mixed periods. It does not measure regulatory outcomes as of May 2024.
The establishment notice shows the board is advisory only and that the Secretary appoints its members. This limits any inference of capture but does not rule it out.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows that industry has access and channels of influence. No item supplies a representative population of AI regulatory institutions or decisions that would show whether capture was or was not the usual pattern as of 2024-05-26. Attempts to obtain EU counterevidence failed. The evidence does not settle the claim.

semantics.note: The normalisation keeps 'appears', the Senators scope, the accurate no-direct-equity report, and both omitted interests. The factual omissions are stated firmly; 'appears' softens only the charge of misleading.

contract.note: It is fair to treat omission as enough without proof of intent. Whether the Startup Fund counts as a personal financial holding depends on separating ownership from economic interest, a distinction the speaker did not draw.

evidence.note: The official transcript shows Altman said he had no equity and did not mention YC or the Startup Fund in that exchange. The source type is labelled official_statistics, but it is a hearing record.
TIME, December 2023, reports an indirect investment in OpenAI through his stake in YC. This supports the YC holding near the relevant period.
2026 courtroom reporting, before the cutoff, records Altman admitting economic exposure through a YC fund and that he did not mention it in the testimony.

Reuters confirms that Altman owned the Startup Fund until March 2024, which supports the omitted ownership. It also relays OpenAI's denial of any financial interest, a company statement and not an independent finding.

reviews.rationale: The YC part holds: Altman said he had no equity, did not mention the indirect YC exposure, and later admitted that exposure. The Startup Fund part is only partly established. He owned the fund at the time of the hearing and did not mention it, but the contract requires economic exposure for the financial implication, and the packet has only OpenAI's denial and no beneficial-interest records.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post.

semantics.note: The normalisation keeps 'traded on' openness and the knowledge by May 2016. It leaves out 'called itself open', which is trivially true. The separate sentence about Altman declining to correct the impression is correctly excluded.

contract.note: Treating knowledge by the leaders as the company's knowledge, and 'traded on' as public positioning, is an ordinary and fair reading.

evidence.note: Contemporaneous reporting of the May 2016 meeting: Altman acknowledged that the expected source-code release went beyond their plans and chose not to correct the impression.
The founding announcement is a company statement used only for what OpenAI publicly said. It promoted publishing, code, shared patents and free collaboration, which shows openness positioning.
In December 2015 Karpathy publicly called the name a misnomer. This shows awareness even earlier than May 2016, but also some public qualification of the openness.

reviews.rationale: OpenAI publicly positioned itself around openness, and in May 2016 its leaders acknowledged that outside expectations of openness exceeded their plans. Karpathy's public caveat shows the limitation was partly acknowledged, but it is consistent with the claim that they knew by May 2016.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post.

semantics.note: A compound claim: the filing and its mission language, roughly half of profits to Microsoft, and a hedged ('seem') safety assessment. The normalisation keeps the qualifiers.

contract.note: Separating an annual Form 990 from an application for exempt status is a literal reading of 'filed for'; it is defensible but strict. Requiring executed agreements for the profit share is fair, because the speaker gave no source or accounting basis.

evidence.note: OpenAI Inc.'s 2022 Form 990, filed November 2023, contains the quoted mission language. The document is itself an annual return.

Available before the cutoff, this secondary summary of IRS data identifies the filing as an annual Form 990 and dates the exemption to 2016. That contradicts describing it as filing for exempt status.
Fortune, January 2023, reports a staged entitlement of 75% falling to 49% from documents it saw. It is a press estimate, with no executed agreement and an unclear applicable stage.
Leike's May 2024 post is firsthand support for the hedged view that safety was deprioritised. It is an individual's statement, not a company disclosure or an audit of resources.

reviews.rationale: The mission language in the November 2023 filing holds. Describing that filing as filing for tax-exempt status is inaccurate, because it was an annual return from an organisation exempt since 2016. The 'almost half' profit share rests only on a press estimate without a verified basis, so it is unresolved. The hedged safety clause has firsthand support but is not scored as a firm claim.
